abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p:
Flexible loops within enzyme active sites are central to substrate binding, transition‐state stabilization, and catalytic turnover. Hydrophobic interactions modulate ligand recognition and influence protein function. Here, we interrogated loop‐mediated hydrophobic contributions to catalysis in 3α‐hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/carbonyl reductase (3α‐HSD/CR) from Comamonas testosteroni. Residue L193 on the flexible substrate‐binding loop was substituted with amino acids spanning a hydrophobicity gradient (W, I, F, M, V, P, A, T, G). Differential scanning fluorimetry showed comparable melting temperatures among variants, indicating minimal effects on global thermal stability. Steady‐state kinetics revealed decreased catalytic efficiency with reduced side‐chain hydrophobicity and corresponding increases in activation free energy (ΔG
‡ ). With the exception of L193W, L193I, L193F, L193P, and L193T, log(k
cat
/K
M ) correlated linearly and positively with residue hydrophobicity, supporting a key role of hydrophobic interactions involving L193 in stabilizing the transition state of androsterone in the 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction. Truncated substrates (2‐decalol, cyclohexanol) cause a significant decrease in catalytic efficiency, exhibiting similar trends with shallower slopes, consistent with predominant L193 close to the steroid A‐ring. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that NAD+ and substrate binding promote loop closure and strengthen hydrophobic interactions involving L193 in the active site. These data establish that the hydrophobic interaction of residue 193 with the transition state of substrate, linked to remote binding interactions of the loop with the unreactive portion of the substrate, significantly contributes to 3α‐HSD/CR catalysis.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions by stabilizing transition states and lowering activation energy, while maintaining high specificity. In the meantime, some enzymes change conformation significantly during their catalytic cycles. Flexible active‐site loops frequently participate in binding with the ligands, facilitate a reaction by an optimal interaction with the transition state, and release the products (Callender & Dyer, 2015; Hammes et al., 2011; Ma & Nussinov, 2010; Pauling, 1948; Richard et al., 2018; Schramm et al., 2008). Upon binding of the substrate, the enzyme undergoes a conformational change from the inactive, unliganded open form to a catalytically active closed form, thereby stabilizing the enzymatic reaction transition state via the induced‐fit model (Hegazy & Richard, 2025a; Richard, 2019). In contrast, some enzymes exist in multiple conformations, and ligand binding stabilizes the active conformation, thereby shifting the population toward the active state through a conformational‐selection mechanism (Boehr et al., 2009; Weikl & Paul, 2014). The binding energy from the interaction of the enzyme with the substrate in the active site can be utilized to correctly position the reactive portion of a substrate relative to the functional groups by favorable ionic, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals, and hydrophobic interactions of the transition state to lower the activation energy of the chemical reaction. Meanwhile, the binding energy from the flexible substrate‐binding loop with the non‐reacting portions of the substrate can be used for inducing the conformational change to close the loops, in which waters are excluded from the active site, and making enhanced interaction with the transition state to increase the rate for the reaction (Amyes et al., 2001; Amyes et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2014; Jencks, 1975; Johnson et al., 2016; Leemhuis et al., 2002; Leferink et al., 2014; Whitty et al., 1995; Wolfenden & Snider, 2001). Despite extensive evidence, the precise contribution of loop‐associated hydrophobic interactions to catalysis remains incompletely defined.

Hydrophobic interactions have been implicated in the structural stability, specificity, and catalysis of enzymes (Estell et al., 1986; Kulkarni et al., 2017; Ponnuswamy, 1993; Richard et al., 2016; Rose & Wolfenden, 1993). Hydrophobic interactions result from the tendency of nonpolar amino acids to aggregate and avoid aqueous environments, thereby creating stable hydrophobic cores within proteins and enzymes. This tendency results in burying hydrophobic residues, which can stabilize the folded state and bind with the nonpolar portion of ligands. Hence, optimal hydrophobic interactions within enzyme active sites are crucial for substrate binding and specificity, and for stabilizing the transition states, thus enhancing catalytic efficiency. Modifying either the hydrophobicity of the enzyme's binding site or substrate by altering the amino acid residues has been demonstrated to have a significant impact on catalytic efficiency in subtilisin and chymotrypsin (Estell et al., 1986; Hansch & Coats, 1970; Wangikar et al., 1995). To quantitatively characterize the hydrophobicity of amino acids, different methodologies have been conducted by measuring the propensity of these residues to transition from aqueous to hydrophobic environments, such as organic solution, the transmembrane region of a protein, and theoretical calculation (Fauchere & Pliska, 1983; Kyte & Doolittle, 1982; Radzicka & Wolfenden, 1988; Simm et al., 2016; Wimley & White, 1996; Zhao & London, 2006). These different approaches give various hydrophobic scales with significant differences among scales, which causes difficulty in elucidating their role in enzyme catalysis quantitatively. To mimic amino acids in the peptide structure, Fauchère and Pliska quantified amino acid hydrophobicity by measuring the partitioning of N‐acetyl‐amino‐acid amides in an octanol/water system compared to that for glycine. This study gives the hydrophobic parameters (πR) of the side chains of the 20 amino acids and the related free energy for transfer for each amino acid measured from H2O to octanol relative to glycine (Fauchere & Pliska, 1983). Thereby, the value of πR may provide a basis for evaluating binding energy from the hydrophobic interaction involved in enzyme catalysis.

The conformational changes of a flexible substrate‐binding loop have been observed in the short‐chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily. These enzymes typically exhibit disordered loops in apo structures that adopt defined conformations upon cofactor and substrate binding (Amaral et al., 2017; Benach et al., 1999; Ladenstein et al., 2008; Savino et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 1996). These changes in loop conformation upon substrate binding are consistent with the induced fit model, in which binding with reactants induces the conformation changes and arranges into a form suitable for transition‐state formation, and implicates their involvement in enzyme catalysis. However, the precise contribution of loop–substrate hydrophobic interactions in SDR catalysis remains unclear. 3α‐Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/carbonyl reductase (3α‐HSD/CR) from Comamonas testosteroni (E.C. 1.1.1.50) is a member of SDR superfamily that oxidizes androsterone with NAD+ via a steady‐state ordered Bi Bi mechanism, in which NAD+ binds first and NADH is released last (Chang et al., 2007; Hwang et al., 2013; Skalhegg, 1975) (Figure 1a,b). Catalysis proceeds through deprotonation of the C3 hydroxyl group of androsterone by the conserved residue Y155, enabling hydride transfer to the C4 position of the NAD+ nicotinamide ring (Hwang et al., 2005). Crystal structures reveal a flexible substrate‐binding loop (residues P185–P219) with an unresolved region spanning residues of 188TETPLLQAGLQDPRYGESIAK208 in the apoenzyme (Chang et al., 2009; Grimm et al., 2000). Structure prediction by the program AlphaFold3 (https://alphafoldserver.com/) suggests that this loop adopts a helix‐turn‐helix fold, and hydrophobicity analysis identifies L193 residue as the most nonpolar position based on the F.P. hydrophobic scale through the ProtScale program (Figure 1c,d). Together with the hydrophobic nature of androsterone, this system provides a suitable model for quantifying the role of hydrophobic interactions of a flexible substrate‐binding loop with a hydrophobic substrate in enzyme catalysis.

sec.p: Here, we investigated the contribution of L193 to 3α‐HSD/CR catalysis by substituting it with residues spanning a hydrophobicity gradient (W, I, F, M, V, P, A, T, G). Catalytic efficiencies were determined for androsterone and truncated analogs (2‐decalol and cyclohexanol) to evaluate both local and distal loop–substrate interactions. We further examined protein stability using differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) and loop dynamics using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. These integrated approaches reveal that hydrophobic packing between L193 on the P185–P219 loop and the nonreacting steroid framework stabilizes the closed, catalytically competent conformation and, together with distal substrate contacts, lowers the effective activation barrier for hydride transfer, thereby increasing catalytic efficiency in 3α‐HSD/CR.

sec.title: Mutagenesis, overexpression, and purification of wild‐type (WT) and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs
sec.p: Site‐directed mutagenesis was performed using the QuickChange Site‐Directed Mutagenesis Kit with Pfu polymerase and the pET15b‐3α‐HSD/CR plasmid as template. Mutants of L193W, L193I, L193F, L193M, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, L193G, R201A, and Y202A 3α‐HSD/CRs were cloned and transformed into Escherichia coli BL21 cells. The desired mutations were verified by DNA sequencing. WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs were overexpressed in E. coli BL21 cells and purified by Ni2+‐chelate chromatography using an imidazole step gradient in 0.15 M NaCl, 50 mM phosphate at pH 7.4. Each expressed enzyme appeared pure and homogenous, confirmed by the SDS‐PAGE (Figure S1).

sec.title: Catalytic efficiency of the WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs acting on the truncated substrates
sec.p:
We studied the effect of mutation at L193 on the catalytic efficiency of 3α‐HSD/CRs through steady‐state kinetics for the truncated substrates, 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol. Mutants of L193W, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G 3α‐HSD/CRs cannot be saturated with the concentration of 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol within their solubility limits of ~7 mM and ~250 mM, respectively, under our assay conditions (pH 10.5, 25°C). Thereby, initial rates proportional to the low concentrations of 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol were measured at several fixed concentrations of NAD+ (Figure S2B,C). The initial rate patterns for the WT and mutants of L193W, L193I, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G 3α‐HSD/CRs show that the lines intersect on the ordinate in a double‐reciprocal plot, consistent with a rapid equilibrium ordered mechanism (Figure 2b,c). Initial rate data were fit to Equation (3) for the WT and mutants of L193I, L193F, and L193M variants, whereas initial rate data were fit to Equation (4) for L193W, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G variants. The obtained kinetic parameters for the WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs catalyzed the reaction of NAD+ with 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol are shown in Tables 1 and S1. These mutants significantly decrease the activity for 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol in comparison with that for androsterone. Compared to the WT 3α‐HSD/CR, the k

sec.title: Effect of hydrophobicity at position 193 on catalytic efficiency and activation energy of the 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction
sec.p: We then investigated the role of the hydrophobic interactions of residues with substrate in the active site in the 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction. We adopted the hydrophobicity parameter (πR) from the study of Fauchère and Pliska, which quantified amino acid hydrophobicity based on distribution coefficients (D) by measuring the partitioning of N‐acetyl‐amino‐acid amides for the side chains of the 20 amino acids between n‐octanol and water. The hydrophobic parameter (πR) represents the difference in log D values between a modified side chain and glycine, and provides the related free energy for transfer for each amino acid measured from H2O to octanol relative to glycine. A greater partitioning of N‐acetyl‐amino‐acid amides into the n‐octanol phase corresponds to a higher log D value and a larger πR value, characterized by increased hydrophobicity. To prevent generating additional H‐bonds, extra‐electrostatic interactions, and unpaired charges in the active site, which may interfere with the hydrophobic interaction investigated in the enzyme reaction, we replaced L193 with the amino acid residues of W, I, F, M, V, P, A, T, and G with different hydrophobic side chains for the study. The relative hydrophobicity parameters (πR) for the side chains of L, W, I, F, M, V, P, A, T, and G are 1.7, 2.25, 1.8, 1.79, 1.23, 1.22, 0.72, 0.31, 0.26, and 0, respectively (Fauchere & Pliska, 1983). For the L193I variant, the side‐chain hydrophobicity is comparable to WT, but its geometry differs. In contrast, the L193T variant has a side‐chain shape similar to L193A, yet it may form additional hydrogen bonds with active‐site residues.

A plot of the log(k
cat
/K

The data were fit to Equation (6), yielding a slope of 1.8 ± 0.2 (R 2 = 0.95). Similar linear relations were observed for 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol, with reduced slopes of 1.3 ± 0.1 (R 2 = 0.98) and 0.9 ± 0.2 (R 2 = 0.84), respectively. The result indicates that the catalytic efficiency of 3α‐HSD/CR is affected by the hydrophobicity of both residue 193 and substrate. The decrease in k

Given that 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol lack CD‐ and BCD‐rings of steroid, respectively, these trends indicate that the remote binding interaction linked to the role of residue 193, which mainly interacts with the A‐ring of the steroid scaffold, and emphasize that the hydrophobicity at loop residue 193 plays a crucial role in 3α‐HSD/CR catalysis.

sec.title: Thermal stability of 3α‐HSD/CR variants
sec.p:
We investigated the effect of the mutation at L193 on the thermal stability of 3α‐HSD/CR variants by DSF at pH 7.0. The predicted pI of 3α‐HSD/CR is 7.21, as calculated using the ExPASy ProtParam tool. DSF was performed at pH 7 to maintain structural integrity, whereas catalytic turnover in the WT enzyme and variants is optimized at pH 10.5. DSF was not intended to replicate catalytic conditions but to probe global folding stability across variants. The thermal unfolding profiles of the WT and mutants of L193W, L193I, L193F, L193M, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G 3α‐HSD/CRs exhibited sigmoidal curves, indicating cooperative unfolding behavior (Figure S4). These results suggest a two‐state transition from the native state (N) to the denatured state (U). The melting temperature (T
m ) at the midpoint of the unfolding curve represents the temperature at which 50% of the protein population is in a denatured state. Equation (7) was fit to the fluorescence data to obtain T
m and ΔH
m (Table S2). The T
m values for WT, L193W, L193I, L193F, L193M, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G 3α‐HSD/CRs are 53.1°C, 52.5°C, 52.0°C, 52.3°C, 52.5°C, 52.4°C, 52.6°C, 52.1°C, 52.3°C, and 52.7°C, respectively, indicating that mutation at L193 situated on the base of the flexible substrate loop has little effect on the thermal stability of 3α‐HSD/CR variants.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulations of WT and mutants of 3α‐HSD/CRs
sec.p: To further validate the mechanism involved in hydrophobic interactions of a substrate with residue L193 on the flexible substrate‐binding loop, which contributes to 3α‐HSD/CR catalytic efficiency, we performed MD simulations of WT 3α‐HSD/CRs, including the apo‐form, binary, and ternary complexes. In addition, the ternary complexes for L193A, L193W, and L193P 3α‐HSD/CRs were also performed to evaluate the effects of the substitutions at residue 193 on the structural conformational changes and binding orientations of the substrate. Since the substrate‐binding loop in the crystal structures of the apo‐form and NAD+‐bound binary complex of 3α‐HSD/CR (PDB ID: 1fjh and 1fk8, respectively) was not resolved, the initial conformations of this region were constructed based on homologous structures prior to MD simulations. We performed structure simulations and analysis of WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs using the Amber package with the Amber force field FF19SB applied in the topology of the enzyme to understand the conformation of the substrate‐binding loop and its interactions with substrate. Simulations of the ternary complexes of WT and L193A, L193W, and L193P mutants were performed with restraints between NAD+ and the substrate to ensure the substrate was consistently bound to the active site throughout the simulations.

The stability of each simulated model was determined by calculating all‐atom RMSD for WT and the mutants of L193A, L193W, and L193P 3α‐HSD/CRs. The simulations were performed in triplicate for each system for 100 ns, except the WT‐NAD+ binary complex for 200 ns. The WT and mutant structures were stable during the simulation and showed smaller RMSD values for the ternary complex compared to the apoenzyme and NAD+‐bound binary complex, while a similar RMSD value was observed for the ternary complex of WT and mutant enzymes (Figure S5). The results show that the substrate‐binding loop is less flexible upon substrate binding. To examine how substrate binding and mutation at residue L193 influence the flexibility of the substrate‐binding loop of 3α‐HSD/CR, the root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) values of backbone atoms were calculated for each residue over the course of the MD trajectories for both WT and mutant enzymes (Figure S6). The simulation of the apoenzyme revealed two major regions with Cα RMSF values greater than 1.5 Å, including G147‐E148 and P191‐I206. The highest RMSF peak corresponded to residue R201, located within the substrate‐binding loop, with an average value of 4.1 Å in the apoenzyme. This peak decreased to 3.4 Å and 1.9 Å in the binary and ternary complexes, respectively. These results are consistent with the increased backbone mobility of the substrate‐binding loop (P185‐K208) observed in the apoenzyme, which corresponds to the unresolved region (T188‐K208) in the crystal structure. The higher RMSF values reflect greater loop flexibility during MD simulations; therefore, the reduced RMSF of the substrate‐binding loop in the ternary complex likely indicates that substrate binding stabilizes the loop in a closed conformation. Furthermore, comparison of RMSF values for residue R201 among the ternary complexes WT‐NAD+‐androsterone, WT‐NAD+‐2‐decalol, WT‐NAD+‐cyclohexanol, and L193A‐NAD+‐androsterone showed only slight variations, with values of 1.9, 1.7, 2.3, and 1.8 Å, respectively, but increase to 2.9 Å for both L193P and L193W ternary complexes.

The simulated structures of the WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs show that the intraprotein contacts made in the core of the protein are almost identical. The main structural and dynamic differences are confined to the substrate‐binding loop dynamics. In the simulations, the substrate‐binding loop appears as a helix‐turn‐helix secondary structure and exhibits significant dynamics in the WT and the mutants of L193A, L193W, and L193P 3α‐HSD/CRs (Figure 4). The substrate‐binding loop appears in the open state (EO) in the active site of the apoenzyme and in the closed states in the binary (E'C) and ternary (EC) complexes of the WT enzyme, which are involved in the formation of the hydrogen bonding between the residues Y202 and N152 and the salt bridge between the residues R201 and E148 (Figure 4b). The closed form in the active site is formed in the binary complex, where residue L193 is involved in the hydrophobic interaction with the nicotinamide of NAD+. In addition, residue L193, which interacts with I206 in the substrate‐binding loop in the apoenzyme, is repositioned to contact both androsterone and the nicotinamide ring, while the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond and R201‐E148 salt bridge are formed in the ternary complexes of WT‐NAD+‐androsterone. Our results support the emerging view that cofactor binding energy in dehydrogenases can be utilized to drive conformational reorganization that stabilizes a catalytically competent active‐site configuration for hydride transfer, analogous to recent proposals for other NAD‐dependent systems, such as glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphite dehydrogenase, and formate dehydrogenase (Cristobal et al., 2023; Hegazy et al., 2024; Hegazy & Richard, 2025b).

sec.p: Binding the truncated substrates, 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol, slightly alters the closed conformation of the substrate‐binding loop, revealing differential interactions of L193 with NAD+ and the truncated substrates. The hydrogen bonding between the residues Y202 and backbone NH of N152 is observed for WT‐NAD+‐2‐decalol and the salt bridge of R201 and E148 formed in the WT‐NAD+‐cyclohexanol, respectively (Figure 4c,d). The distances between these interactions are shown in Table 2. Since Y155 acts as a general base to abstract the proton from the hydroxyl group at C3 of androsterone, and L193 mainly interacts with the A‐ring of androsterone, we measured the distance between the Cα carbon of residues 155 and 193 to probe the loop's conformational state. In the apoenzyme, this distance is the greatest at 18.1 Å in an open conformation. Upon binding of NAD+ and androsterone to form binary and ternary complexes, respectively, the substrate binding loop adopts a closed conformation, where the distance between the Cα atoms of residues Y155 and L193 is decreased to 11.8 Å in the ternary complex. The hydrophobic interactions of L193 are formed with the proximal hydrophobic region of androsterone. Replacement of leucine by alanine weakened hydrophobic contacts with the substrate, increased the distance between residue A193 and the A‐ring of androsterone. L193A mutant remains in the closed form with the hydrogen bonding interaction of Y202 and N152, but the salt bridge of R201 and E148 in the tip of the substrate‐binding loop is disrupted, and the distance between the Cα atoms of residues Y155 and A193 increased (Figure 4e,f).

sec.p: Replacing L193 with tryptophan increases the side‐chain volume at position 193. The indole ring shifts toward the nicotinamide ring, thereby alleviating steric clash with androsterone between the indole ring and the substrate. The L193W variant remains predominantly in the closed conformation, with the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond and the R201‐E148 salt bridge preserved, as observed in the WT‐NAD+‐androsterone ternary complex (Figure 4g,h). In contrast, replacing L193 with proline disrupts the R201‐E148 salt bridge and the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond at the tip of the substrate‐binding loop, thereby increasing loop dynamics (Figure 4i,j).

sec.title: Functional role of the flexible substrate‐binding loop
sec.p: Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions by stabilizing the transition state relative to the ground‐state substrate, thereby lowering the activation free energy, which can arise from multiple catalytic strategies, including induced fit or substrate strain, as well as general acid–base, metal ion, and electrostatic catalysis mediated by active‐site functional groups (Fersht, 1999). Conformational changes and loop motions are widely implicated in solvent exclusion, the precise positioning of catalytic residues and substrates, the optimization of transition‐state interactions, and the facilitation of product release (Johnson & Holyoak, 2010; Schramm et al., 2008). The shape complementarity between the enzyme and substrate in the active site is a major determinant of binding energy and specificity, and catalysis is promoted by enforcing near‐attack conformations and by forming active‐site cages that are structurally complementary to transition‐state geometries (Bruice & Benkovic, 2000; Fersht, 1999). Substrate‐induced conformational changes from the open inactive conformation (EO) to the closed active conformation (EC) have been characterized in triosephosphate isomerase, glycerol 3‐phosphate dehydrogenase, and orotidine 5'‐monophosphate decarboxylase. In these enzymes, loop and side‐chain motions promote catalysis by stabilizing the closed active state (EC) via the binding energy of direct protein–substrate phosphodianion interactions, the side chain‐side chain packing networks, and reshaping the active‐site microenvironment to favor transition‐state formation (Amyes & Richard, 2013; Hegazy & Richard, 2025a; Hegazy & Richard, 2025b; Malabanan et al., 2010; Richard et al., 2018).

Our combined site‐directed mutagenesis, kinetics, DSF, and MD simulations highlight the role of the flexible substrate‐binding loop and hydrophobic interactions in 3α‐HSD/CR catalysis. Crystal structures of apo 3α‐HSD/CR and the NAD+‐bound binary complex show overall similarity but lack resolution of the flexible substrate‐binding loop (Grimm et al., 2000). MD simulations revealed that this loop adopts a helix–turn–helix structure, open in the apoenzyme and closed in both the WT‐NAD+ binary and the WT‐NAD+‐androsterone ternary complexes. Closure of the NAD+ binary complex is critical for subsequent substrate binding, and the ternary complexes display distinct conformations and interactions depending on the substrate. These findings are consistent with an ordered Bi Bi kinetic mechanism, in which NAD+ binds first and induces the conformational closure that prepares the active site for substrate entry. In the WT ternary complex with androsterone, the NAD+ nicotinamide ring reorients toward androsterone to enable hydride transfer in the reaction. The hydrophobic side‐chain of L193 modulates the local environment together with a salt bridge between R201 and E148 to stabilize the loop closure in the WT‐NAD+ binary complex. Upon binding with androsterone, L193 moves toward the A‐ring of androsterone, accompanied by an additional Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond. This closed form expels solvent from the active site and enhances hydrophobic packing between L193 and androsterone, which may further provide a force to stabilize the transition state and lower the activation energy for facilitating the reaction. Thus, the flexible loop appears to function as a dynamic gate to permit substrate access when open and shield the active site when closed. R201 and Y202 serve as gatekeepers, forming key salt‐bridge and hydrogen‐bond interactions by interacting with E148 and N152, respectively, to reinforce the closed state. Substituting R201 or Y202 with alanine disrupts these contacts, reducing catalytic efficiency by 2.7 and 38‐fold, respectively. This is consistent with MD simulations of the ternary complex, in which the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond and the R201‐E148 salt bridge stabilize the active closed conformation and help tune the active‐site microenvironment to favor formation of the hydride‐transfer transition state. Y202 plays a more direct role in organizing the catalytically competent closed‐loop state, likely due to its position at the loop tip and closer proximity to the substrate region. In addition to the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond, the aromatic ring of Y202 may contribute to local packing and hydrophobic contacts with the bound androsterone, whereas R201 appears to function primarily through the R201‐E148 interaction network that supports loop closure.

3α‐HSD/CR from Comamonas testosteroni belongs to the short‐chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily. Sequence alignments across SDR enzymes typically reveal low overall sequence identity but conservation of motifs, including the N‐terminal Gly‐X3‐Gly‐X‐Gly cofactor‐binding sequence and the catalytically important Ser‐Tyr‐Lys‐Asn tetrad, whereas the substrate‐binding loop is among the most divergent regions (Filling et al., 2002; Kallberg et al., 2002). To assess conservation within bacterial 3α‐hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, we retrieved protein sequences from Gram‐negative species in the NCBI Reference Sequence database (RefSeq, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/RefSeq) and performed multiple‐sequence alignment. Notably, L193, R201, and Y202 within the substrate‐binding loop are highly conserved among Gram‐negative orthologs (Figure S7), supporting a functionally important role for this loop region. Broader phylogenetic analyses of more distantly related homologs will be needed to determine whether these residues govern active‐site loop function more generally.

sec.title: Role of L193 in catalysis
sec.p: ProtScale analysis of loop residues L192‐K208 identified L193 as the most hydrophobic position. To probe its catalytic role, we generated L193W, L193I, L193F, L193M, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G variants and evaluated their reactions with androsterone and truncated analogs. All variants displayed similar melting temperatures, indicating little effect on the thermal stability of 3α‐HSD/CR. Compared to androsterone, 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol lack the CD‐ring and BCD‐ring of the steroid skeleton, respectively, which may decrease the hydrophobic interaction in the remote binding interaction with the substrate‐binding loop.

MD simulations show that the active site loop undergoes a substrate‐induced conformational change to a closed, active state, and substitutions at L193 differentially affect this state. Thus, mutagenesis by these hydrophobic residue substitutions can affect the shape complementarity between the enzyme and the substrate, change the loop conformations in the ordered and disordered states during substrate binding, and the rate of hydride transfer in the transition state. Future stopped‐flow binding kinetics will be required to determine the rates of the conformation transitions. Mutation at residue 193 of 3α‐HSD/CR affects the binding of NAD+, androsterone, 2‐decalol, and cyclohexanol in the active site. Compared to WT, catalyzing the reaction of NAD+ with androsterone, the dissociation constant (K
iA ) is increased for the mutants from 1.1‐fold for the L193I mutant to 5.7‐fold for the L193G mutant, except for the L193F mutant with a 2.4‐fold decrease. The plot of log(K
iA ) versus hydrophobicity at residue 193 shows a scattered distribution with a weak linear relationship (data not shown). The K
M value cannot be determined for mutants of L193I, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G variants with androsterone, and for mutants of L193W, L193V, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G variants with 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol due to the solubility limit. The results suggest that the mutation alters the loop conformation involved in the substrate binding. The failure to reach saturation within the accessible substrate concentration range is consistent with a substantially increased apparent K
M , which may result from amino acid substitution–dependent steric mismatch, altered packing, or changes in local polarity.

The rate‐limiting step of hydride transfer in the WT enzyme has been previously established by kinetic isotope effect studies under similar reaction conditions (Hwang et al., 2017). Although direct kinetic isotope effect measurements were not conducted for all L193 variants in the present study, the intersection of the family lines in the Lineweaver‐Burk plot suggests a conserved catalytic sequence across variants (Figure 2, Table S1). Kinetic analysis of mutants showed that initial‐rate patterns for L193F, L193M, and L193V 3α‐HSD/CR variants followed a steady‐state ordered mechanism, whereas L193W, L193I, L193P, L193A, L193T, and L193G mutants displayed a rapid‐equilibrium ordered mechanism for androsterone oxidation. With truncated substrates (2‐decalol and cyclohexanol), all variants, including WT, followed rapid‐equilibrium ordered mechanisms, which indicates that the rate of the chemical step is far lower than the release of NAD+ from the E‐NAD+ binary complex.

Thus, the hydrophobic contribution of residue 193 likely influences both TS stabilization and the free energy landscape of ES formation. In all cases, catalytic efficiencies decreased, corresponding to higher activation energies for the reaction (Table 1). Thereby, ΔG

These results indicate the critical role of hydrophobic interactions involving L193 in stabilizing the transition state of hydride transfer from androsterone to NAD+ in the 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction, and L193 contributes primarily through hydrophobic contacts with the steroid A‐ring. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that certain L193 mutations alter the rate of conformational reorganization of the loop rather than hydride transfer itself. Future stopped‐flow or KIE experiments will be required to determine whether hydride transfer remains rate‐limiting for each variant.

We performed MD simulations of 3α‐HSD/CR. The average distance of Cα‐C4 (L193‐NAD+ nicotinamide) and Cα‐C3 (L193‐androsterone) in the WT‐NAD+‐androsterone ternary complex is 8.7 and 8.0 Å, respectively, which suggests that L193 does not directly contact the catalytic center. Accordingly, we propose that L193 modulates catalysis primarily through indirect, conformational, and environmental effects. L193 residue stabilizes the closed, catalytically competent substrate‐binding loop and thereby tunes the local packing and physicochemical environment surrounding the NAD+ nicotinamide ring and bound androsterone during the hydride‐transfer step. The side‐chain substitutions at position 193 could alter the reaction barrier by shifting the population and stability of the closed state and by subtly reorganizing the local electrostatic and hydrophobic milieu that supports productive substrate and cofactor positioning and catalytic residue alignment.

The apparent exceptions observed for substitutions with tryptophan, phenylalanine, isoleucine, threonine, and proline can be rationalized by considering side‐chain geometry and polarity in addition to hydrophobicity. Isoleucine has hydrophobicity and volume similar to leucine, yet L193I reduces catalytic efficiency (k
cat
/K
M ) by ~10‐fold and cannot be saturated by androsterone, consistent with a loss of shape complementarity required for productive binding and transition‐state formation in 3α‐HSD/CR catalysis. Likewise, the bulkier aromatic substitutions perturb packing in the binding pocket: L193F and L193W increase K
M by 2.3‐ and 7.1‐fold, respectively, and decrease k
cat
/K
M by 2.3‐ and 29‐fold, respectively, consistent with steric constraints that impair productive substrate positioning. In contrast, L193V exhibits high catalytic performance (k
cat
/K
M = 2.0 × 107 M−1 s−1; K
M = 40 μM). Replacing Val with Thr preserves a similar side‐chain size but introduces a polar hydroxyl group. Accordingly, L193T decreases k
cat
/K
M by 3.4‐fold and also cannot be saturated by androsterone, suggesting that the T193 hydroxyl group disrupts hydrophobic packing and introduces unfavorable interactions in the steroid‐binding pocket. Proline provides a distinct case. Because L193 lies within a helix–turn–helix motif, introducing Pro at this position is expected to distort local helical geometry rather than rigidify the substrate‐binding loop (Bright & Sansom, 2003). Consistent with the loss of the R201‐E148 salt bridge and the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond (Figure 4i,j), this structural perturbation likely increases loop flexibility and destabilizes the closed, catalytically competent conformation, preventing optimal alignment of the substrate and catalytic groups for hydride transfer and thereby causing a pronounced decrease in catalytic efficiency.

Overall, while hydrophobicity accounts for the general trend in catalytic efficiency, geometric compatibility is essential for orienting androsterone within the binding pocket. Bulky residues of W and F likely impose steric penalties that reduce packing efficiency, whereas polar substitutions of T can disrupt the hydrophobic microenvironment. Thus, hydrophobicity and shape complementarity jointly determine substrate binding and transition‐state stabilization.

A plot of ΔG
‡ versus πR of the side chain at residue 193 yielded reverse linear relations for androsterone, 2‐decalol, and cyclohexanol with slopes of −2.4 ± 0.3, −1.7 ± 0.1, and − 1.2 ± 0.3, respectively. This demonstrates that increasing side‐chain hydrophobicity decreases the activation energy, with the greatest sensitivity for androsterone. Because πR represents the free‐energy change for transfer of amino acid side chains from water to octanol relative to glycine, the slopes indicate that decreases in the activation energy are proportional to the side‐chain hydrophobicity. The reduction in ΔG
‡ was approximately 2.4‐, 1.7‐, and 1.2‐fold as large as the free energy of transfer of straight chain groups of N‐acetyl‐amino‐acid amides from water to n‐octanol for androsterone, 2‐decalol, and cyclohexanol, respectively. Thus, higher hydrophobicity at L193 lowers the activation energy by enhancing enzyme–transition‐state interactions. We have demonstrated that the WT 3α‐HSD/CR acting on 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol significantly decreases catalytic efficiency due to the loss of remote binding energy (Hwang et al., 2017). The smaller slopes for truncated substrates reflect loss of remote binding interactions provided by the CD‐ and BCD‐rings of androsterone. These rings contribute to catalysis by stabilizing the transition state through loop interactions, linking flexible‐loop closure and hydrophobic contacts to transition‐state stabilization in enzyme catalysis.

MD simulations of 3α‐HSD/CR reveal that the substrate‐binding loop (P185–P219) samples distinct open and closed conformations. We propose a model (Figure 6) in which hydrophobic interactions between the substrate‐binding loop (P185–P219) and the substrate stabilize the closed loop conformation (EC), thereby shifting the equilibrium away from the open inactive form (EO). MD simulations show that the substrate‐binding loop in an open conformation of apoenzyme (EO) changes to a closed conformation in the NAD+‐bound binary complex (E'CA). This conformational change is required to properly position active‐site residues for subsequent androsterone binding and to promote further closure of the substrate‐binding loop, yielding the closed ECAB ternary complex. Within this induced‐fit model, the kinetic parameter K
iA reflects both NAD+ binding and the accompanying conformational transition to E'CA. Substitutions at L193 are expected to modulate hydrophobic contacts and perturb local loop packing and interaction networks within the active site, thereby altering the stability of E'CA and shifting K
iA . Meanwhile, the k
cat/
K
M for androsterone reflects the composite process spanning androsterone, the ligand‐coupled transition to the closed active ECAB ternary complex, and progression through the hydride‐transfer step leading to androstanedione formation and release. This ligand‐driven loop closure is proposed to lower the activation free energy primarily by improving active‐site organization rather than through direct transition‐state contact. Accordingly, L193 mutations that destabilize the closed E'C and EC conformations are predicted to increase K
iA and K
M for androsterone and to reduce catalytic efficiency (k

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p:
This study demonstrates that residue L193, located on the flexible substrate‐binding loop of 3α‐HSD/CR, plays a central role in catalysis through hydrophobic interactions and shape complementarity with bound steroid substrates. Site‐directed mutagenesis of L193 to residues spanning a hydrophobicity gradient revealed that catalytic efficiency (k
cat
/K
M ) scales directly with side‐chain hydrophobicity, whereas the activation free energy (ΔG
‡ ) decreases proportionally. Comparative analyses with truncated substrates of 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol showed reduced catalytic efficiencies and smaller slopes in hydrophobicity‐activity correlations, indicating that L193 primarily interacts with the steroid A‐ring, while distal rings contacts provide additional binding energy for the stabilization of the transition state. Importantly, variants that deviate from simple hydrophobicity trends underscore the role of shape complementarity, in which changes in side‐chain size, branching, or polarity can impose steric constraints or disrupt packing, thereby impairing productive substrate orientation in both the ground state and the transition state. Thus, hydrophobicity contributes to stabilization of the closed active form, but optimal catalysis requires a geometrically compatible packing interface between L193, the loop, and the steroid. Thermal stability assays confirmed that substitutions at L193 did not affect global protein folding, emphasizing that observed effects were functional rather than structural.

MD simulations revealed that the substrate‐binding loop adopts a helix–turn–helix conformation, remaining open in the apoenzyme and closed in binary and ternary complexes. Our findings indicate that the P185–P219 loop is a key driver of substrate‐induced conformational change that activates the enzyme. Loop closure creates a catalytically competent active site by excluding solvent, reorganizes the local electrostatic and hydrophobic environment, repositions the NAD+ nicotinamide, and stabilizes hydrophobic contacts between L193 and the substrate. In addition, the Y202‐N152 hydrogen bond and the R201‐E148 salt bridge reinforce the closed, catalytically competent state, linking local interaction networks to conformational gating and to the maintenance of a properly shaped binding pocket. Substitution of leucine by alanine disrupted these interactions, weakened loop–substrate packing, and increased loop mobility.

Collectively, these results support a model in which hydrophobic contacts and shape‐complementary packing between L193 and the enzyme‐bound steroid stabilize the active closed form (EC) relative to the open form (EO), thereby activating 3α‐HSD/CR for catalysis. This work highlights the critical contribution of loop‐associated hydrophobicity to enzyme catalysis, where the P185–P219 loop functions as a substrate‐responsive gating element that couples binding energy, through both hydrophobicity and geometric compatibility, to the formation of a solvent‐excluded, transition‐state–stabilizing active site optimized for hydride transfer in the 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction.

sec.title: Reagents
sec.p: Androsterone, 2‐decalol, cyclohexanol, and NAD+ were from Sigma‐Aldrich. Sodium 3‐(cyclohexylamino)‐1‐propane sulfonate (CAPS) and 4‐(2‐hydroxyethyl)‐1‐piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) were from Sigma. SYPRO Orange (5000×) was from Thermo Fisher Scientific.

sec.title: Site‐directed mutagenesis of 3α‐HSD/CR variants
sec.p: Variants of L193W, L193F, L193M, L193V, L193P, L193A, and L193G 3αHSD/CRs were generated from the pET15b‐3α‐HSD/CR plasmid using the Quickchange Site‐Directed Mutagenesis kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) with PfuUltra HF DNA polymerase to elongate the oligonucleotide primers during the temperature cycling process. The primers used to create the cDNA encoding the 3α‐HSD/CR mutants are shown in Table S3. The original DNA template was digested using Dpn1 endonuclease, which specifically targets methylated and hemimethylated DNA. The resulting nicked vector DNA, harboring the desired mutations, was then transformed into DH5α competent cells. A plasmid containing the 3α‐HSD/CR gene or its mutant variants was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) cells. The entire set of mutants derived from 3α‐HSD/CR cDNA was sequenced to ensure fidelity.

sec.title: Overexpression, purification, and characterization of 3α‐HSD/CRs
sec.p: Recombinant protein expression was carried out in BL21(DE3) cultures grown in 1 liter of Luria‐Bertani medium supplemented with 100 mg/L ampicillin at 37°C. Protein production was induced by the addition of 0.5 mM isopropyl 1‐thio‐β‐D‐galactopyranoside when the culture reached an optical density (OD) of 0.6–1.0 at 600 nm. Following a 4‐h incubation period, cells were harvested and lysed via sonication. The resulting cell lysates were ultracentrifuged at 8000 g for 20 min, and the supernatant was subsequently applied to a His‐bind nickel‐nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni2+‐NTA) resin column for purification. Proteins were eluted using a stepwise gradient from 0 to 0.5 M imidazole containing 50 mM phosphate, 0.15 M NaCl at pH 7.4. The fractions containing His‐tagged 3α‐HSD/CR were pooled and extensively dialyzed against dialysis buffer containing 1 mM EDTA, 10% glycerol, and 10 mM HEPES at pH 7.4. The pure protein was obtained in a homogeneous form, as confirmed by 15% SDS‐PAGE. Protein concentrations were determined spectrophotometrically, using a dimeric form with ε280 = 22,920 M−1 cm−1, as calculated by ProtParam (Wilkins et al., 1999).

sec.title: Steady‐state kinetics
sec.p: The initial rate of the oxidation of androsterone with NAD+ catalyzed by the WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs was measured by monitoring the formation of NADH at 340 nm spectrophotometrically on a Lambda 650 UV/VIS spectrometer (PerkinElmer), utilizing a molar extinction coefficient (ε340) of 6220 M−1 cm−1. Typically, the initial rate pattern for the WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs‐catalyzed reaction was obtained by varying the concentrations of androsterone or the truncated analog of 2‐decalol and cyclohexanol at several fixed concentrations of NAD+ in 0.1 mg/mL BSA and 0.1 M CAPS at pH 10.5 at 25°C. The assay was conducted at pH 10.5 for an optimum 3α‐HSD/CR‐catalyzed reaction (Hwang et al., 2005). Due to differences in activity among the truncated analogs, different amounts of WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs were added for the assay. Typically, the concentrations of WT 3α‐HSD/CR for the assay of androsterone, 2‐decalol, and cyclohexanol are 0.085 nM, 85 nM, and 34 nM, respectively (Hwang et al., 2017). The substrate concentrations were determined three times using an endpoint assay with 3α‐HSD/CR for androsterone and 2‐decalol, and equine alcohol dehydrogenase for cyclohexanol. All reactions were initiated by adding the enzyme.

sec.title: Thermal unfolding of 3α‐HSD/CR
sec.p:
The thermal unfolding of WT and mutant 3α‐HSD/CRs was performed by DSF (Chou et al., 2023). DSF measurements were performed at pH 7.0 to compare global folding stability across variants under near‐neutral conditions and to minimize pH‐driven destabilization effects during thermal unfolding. A solution containing 2 μM 3α‐HSD/CR and 5x SYPRO Orange in 100 mM HEPES buffer at pH 7.0 was dispensed into a 96‐well PCR plate and sealed with an optical adhesive film to minimize evaporation. DSF data were collected using a QuantStudio 3 real‐time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with fluorescence excitation and emission detected via the VIC channel. The thermal denaturation assay was conducted at a heating rate of 0.9°C/min over the temperature range 25°C to 85°C. Fluorescence intensities obtained from the DSF experiments were imported into Microsoft Excel and subsequently analyzed in SigmaPlot 11.0 using the appropriate equations. The baselines for the native and denatured states were determined by selecting linear regions at low and high temperatures, respectively, and were integrated into the fitting process. Fluorescence intensity data were fit to Equation (7) to obtain the T
m and ΔH
m values of 3α‐HSD/CR variants.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulations of apo‐form, binary, and ternary complexes of 3α‐HSD/CR
sec.p: The crystal structure of 3α‐HSD/CR was obtained from RCSB PDB (PDB ID: 1fk8). Since the loop region (residues T188–K208) was not resolved in this structure, it was modeled using a template loop structure from Pseudomonas 3α‐HSD (PDB: 2DKN), based on the high structural similarity between the two homologous enzymes. The 3α‐HSD/CR homologous model was built in Modeller 10.5. Androsterone and 2‐decalol were docked by AutoDock Vina to generate substrate‐bound 3α‐HSD/CR structures. Simulation and analysis were performed utilizing the Amber package of Amber24. The MD simulations were performed three times with different velocities to ensure reliable results. The Amber force field FF19SB was applied in the topology of 3α‐HSD/CR. For substrates, parameters were obtained from the generalized amber force field (GAFF2). An octahedral box of 10 Å was constructed around 3α‐HSD/CR, and the ensemble system was solvated in the TIP3P water model. The protonation state of 3α‐HSD/CR at pH 7 was estimated using the H++ program except for Y155 in the ternary complex, which acts as a general base. The charge of 3α‐HSD/CR was neutralized by 150 mM NaCl as a salt buffer. Minimization was applied for 1000 steps. Enzyme and ligands in the system were restrained on 100 kcal·mol−1·Å−2, followed by heating in 1 ns from 100 to 298 K in NVT, then equilibrating in the NPT ensemble system for 1 ns. A brief minimization of everything was conducted with a 10 kcal·mol−1·Å−2 restraint on Cα atoms. Following the remaining steps for relaxation, the positional restraints decrease on the Cα atoms to 10, then 0.1 kcal·mol−1·Å−2 for 1 ns, respectively. A final unrestrained relaxation of the system was performed for 1 ns. The MD simulations were carried out using the pmemd module of the GPU‐accelerated Amber 24 package. The production MD simulation was performed using 2 fs time steps and the SHAKE algorithm. The cut‐off distance for classical non‐bond interaction was set to 9 Å. The Langevin (collision frequency of 1 ps−1) and Monte Carlo barostat methods were applied for the regulation of temperature and pressure, respectively. The simulation was performed for 100 ns in the NPT ensemble (298 K, 1 atm).

MD simulations of substrate‐bound 3α‐HSD/CR were performed with and without restraints to evaluate the preferred substrate binding pose and the possible interaction modes between active site residues and the substrate. In the restrained MD simulations, 100 ns MD simulations were performed by restraining the C–H distance (3.0 Å) between C4 of nicotinamide and C3‐H of androsterone by applying a harmonic potential of 50 kcal/mol Å−2. These restraints were applied to mimic the near‐attack conformation of the substrate in the hydride transfer pathway from C3‐H of androsterone to C4 of nicotinamide of NAD+ during the reaction.
